summary:
Plateau State is a North Central state in Nigeria with its capital at Jos and a population of around 4.7 million. It stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 criminalises same-sex conduct, bans same-sex cohabitation and public shows of a same-sex amorous relationship, and carries penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment.

Shari'a criminal law does not apply in Plateau State, so the death-penalty exposure that applies in Nigeria's twelve northern states does not apply here; criminal liability rests on national statutory law alone.

Plateau State is not recorded as showing the concentration of arrests and communal tension attributed to the North Central zone.

Nigeria has no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and violence against them is documented as frequent.

A 2022 court challenge ruled Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act unconstitutional and unenforceable anywhere in the country.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement of the national act elsewhere in Nigeria has involved mass arrests at private gatherings and hotels, including more than 100 people at a hotel party in Asaba, Delta State in June 2018, 57 young men at a Lagos hotel in August 2018, 67 people in Warri in August 2023 and 76 people at a Gombe State party in October 2023. No comparable raid in Plateau State is documented in this record.

'Kito' gangs elsewhere in Nigeria lure LGBTQ+ people through dating applications to meetings where they are beaten, filmed and blackmailed under threat of outing; this pattern is documented nationally and a visitor using such applications in Plateau State faces the same exposure.

Police elsewhere in Nigeria have used the law as pretext for extortion, including a March 2025 case in Lagos where a man was struck with a police gun and released only after paying part of a demanded bribe because he 'looked gay'.
localsOnly:
Residents of Plateau State are subject to Nigeria's Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, which criminalises same-sex conduct, cohabitation between same-sex partners, public shows of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment.

Shari'a criminal law does not apply in Plateau State, so the death-penalty provisions operating in Nigeria's twelve northern states do not reach residents here.

Nigeria provides no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and LGBTQ+ Nigerians report fearing medical care and police reporting because of arrest and 'kito' extortion risk.

Proposals to criminalise cross-dressing were reported in September 2022 and were met with fear among transgender Nigerians.

Custody placement for transgender prisoners in Nigeria is decided case by case; press coverage of Bobrisky's April 2024 sentencing publicly asked which prison 'they will keep the crossdresser in', and the available account does not record whether she was held in a male or female section.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2022 ruling striking down Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act has been appealed, upheld or is being enforced in Plateau State is unresolved in this record.

No Plateau State-specific enforcement incidents, arrests or prosecutions under the national act are documented here; the absence of such records does not establish their absence in practice.

Whether Plateau State has any state-level provisions on cross-dressing, gender presentation or public order that could be used against trans visitors is not sourced.
